title: Gases
summary: Learn the relationships between pressure, volume, temperature and moles, the gas laws and real gases.
cards.0.p: Gases compress easily, fill their container and mix in any proportion. Four quantities describe a gas: pressure P, volume V, temperature T and number of moles n. Temperature is always used in kelvins.
cards.0.key: The kelvin temperature is the Celsius temperature plus 273. 0 °C is not zero, it is 273 K. Gases have low densities.
cards.0.once.soru: In gas calculations, how many kelvins is 27 °C?
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: The gas laws work with kelvins. You add 273 to the Celsius value.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: You add 273, you don't subtract it.
cards.1.p: 1 atm equals 760 mmHg and about 101.3 kPa. A manometer measures gas pressure. If the mercury is lower on the gas side, then Pgas = P0 + h.
cards.1.key: 1 atm is 76 cmHg, and 1 mmHg equals 1 torr. If the mercury is higher on the gas side, Pgas = P0 − h. In a closed-end manometer, Pgas = h.
cards.1.once.soru: In an open-end manometer, the mercury is 10 cm lower on the gas side. The outside pressure is 76 cmHg. What is the gas pressure in cmHg?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The gas pushes the mercury harder than the outside air. So it is 76 + 10 = 86.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: The mercury is lower on the gas side, so the gas is pushing harder.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: That would be true for a closed-end manometer.
cards.2.p: At constant temperature and moles, pressure and volume are inversely proportional, and P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂. If the volume is halved, the pressure doubles.
cards.2.key: The particles then hit the walls twice as often. The P–V graph is a hyperbola. A scuba diver doesn't hold their breath while rising, because the air in the lungs expands.
cards.3.p: At constant pressure and moles, volume is directly proportional to kelvin temperature, and V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. The temperature at which the volume would drop to zero is called absolute zero. Absolute zero is 0 K, or −273 °C.
cards.3.key: Heating from 27 °C to 54 °C does not double the volume. The temperature goes from 300 K to 327 K, and the volume grows by only 9%.
cards.4.p: At constant volume and moles, pressure is directly proportional to kelvin temperature, and P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. Heated particles hit the walls more often and harder.
cards.4.key: That's why tire pressure rises on a long drive and why you never throw a spray can into a fire. Don't confuse this law with the law of combining volumes.
cards.5.p: At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles. At constant temperature and pressure, volume is directly proportional to moles, and V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂.
cards.5.svg#0: same T, P and V → same number of particles
cards.5.key: When you blow up a balloon, its volume grows because you add gas. In reactions where the moles of gas decrease, such as N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the volume decreases too.
cards.5.once.soru: Under the same conditions, which has more molecules: 1 L of H₂ or 1 L of O₂?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Under the same conditions, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: O₂ is heavier, but the number of particles is the same.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: H₂ is lighter, but the number of particles is the same.
cards.6.p: If the moles are constant, the three laws combine into P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. You cancel whatever quantity doesn't change from both sides. Temperature must be in kelvins.
cards.6.key: For example, 6 L of gas at 27 °C and 1 atm becomes V₂ = 1·6·400 / (300·2) = 4 L at 127 °C and 2 atm. For P and V it is enough to use the same unit on both sides.
cards.6.once.soru: Both the pressure and the kelvin temperature of a gas double. What happens to its volume?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Doubling the pressure halves the volume, and doubling the temperature doubles it. The two effects cancel.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Raising the pressure shrinks the volume. The two effects work in opposite directions.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Raising the temperature also grows the volume, and the two effects cancel.
cards.7.h: The ideal gas law: PV = nRT
cards.7.p: P·V = n·R·T links all four quantities. If P is in atm, V in liters and T in kelvins, then R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K). In SI units, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
cards.7.etk.soru: P·V = n·R·T, R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K). Change the moles, the temperature and the volume.
cards.7.key: For example, 0.5 mol of gas in a 4.1 L container at 27 °C has a pressure of P = 0.5·0.082·300 / 4.1 = 3 atm. If pressure is in kPa, use R = 8.314 L·kPa/(mol·K).
cards.8.p: If you substitute n = m/M, you get d = P·M/(R·T). Gas density increases with pressure and molar mass and decreases with temperature.
cards.8.key: Using density, the molar mass of an unknown gas is found from M = d·R·T/P.
cards.8.once.soru: Why does a hot air balloon rise?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Heated air has a lower density. The cooler air around it pushes it up.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Hot air has mass too. There is just less of it in the same volume.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The flame heats the air. What lifts the balloon is the difference in density.
cards.9.p: According to kinetic theory, ideal gas particles move randomly, their volume is negligible and they don't attract each other. The average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
cards.9.svg#1: particle volume ≈ 0 · no attraction · elastic collisions
cards.9.key: Collisions between particles are elastic. At the same temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy, but a light gas moves faster.
cards.10.p: A gas spreading through another gas is called diffusion, and a gas escaping through a tiny hole is called effusion. The rate is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass, and r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).
cards.10.svg#6: H₂ spreads √(32/2) = 4 times faster than O₂
cards.10.key: H₂ (2 g/mol) spreads 4 times faster than O₂ (32 g/mol). The comparison is made at the same temperature.
cards.11.h: Dalton's law and gas over water
cards.11.p: Each gas in a mixture exerts pressure as if it filled the container alone, so Ptotal = PA + PB. The partial pressure of a gas is PA = XA·Ptotal.
cards.11.svg#22: water levels inside and outside equal
cards.11.key: XA is the mole fraction of gas A. For a gas collected over water, subtract the water vapor pressure. At 25 °C the water vapor pressure is about 24 mmHg, so H₂ collected at 760 mmHg has a pressure of 736 mmHg.
cards.12.p: Real gas particles have volume and attract each other. So real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure and low temperature. A gas above its critical temperature won't liquefy even when compressed.
cards.12.key: A gas below its critical temperature is called a vapor, and a vapor liquefies when compressed. The most nearly ideal gases are small, nonpolar ones such as He and H₂.
cards.12.once.soru: Under which conditions does a gas behave most like an ideal gas?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: Under these conditions the particles are far apart and fast. So their volume and attraction become negligible.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Under these conditions the particles are crowded and attraction matters.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: At high pressure the particles' own volume becomes important.
cards.13.p:
• Temperature is always in kelvins, and 1 atm is 760 mmHg.
• The gas laws combine into P·V = n·R·T.
• Density is d = P·M/(R·T). By Graham's law, r ∝ 1/√M.
• Average kinetic energy depends only on temperature.
• Total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
quiz.0.q: A closed 8.2 L container holds 0.5 mol of ideal gas at 127 °C. What is the gas pressure in atm? (R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K))
quiz.0.e: T = 127 + 273 = 400 K. P = n·R·T / V = 0.5·0.082·400 / 8.2 = 2 atm. If you forget to convert to kelvins, you get 0.64 atm.
quiz.1.q: Two containers are joined by a closed valve. The 2 L one holds He at 3 atm and the 4 L one holds Ne at 1.5 atm. If the valve is opened at constant temperature, what is the final pressure in atm?
quiz.1.e: Each gas spreads into the total 6 L. P(He) = 3·2/6 = 1 atm and P(Ne) = 1.5·4/6 = 1 atm. By Dalton's law, P(total) = 1 + 1 = 2 atm. In short, you can write P₁V₁ + P₂V₂ = P(final)·V(total).
quiz.2.q: At the same temperature, order these gases from fastest to slowest spreading. (g/mol: H₂ 2, He 4, CH₄ 16, O₂ 32, CO₂ 44)
quiz.2.e: By Graham's law, the rate is inversely proportional to √M, so the gas with the smaller molar mass is faster. The order is H₂ > He > CH₄ > O₂ > CO₂.
quiz.3.q: Hydrogen is collected over water at 27 °C. The water levels inside and outside are equal, and the outside pressure is 750 mmHg. If the vapor pressure of water at 27 °C is 27 mmHg, what is the partial pressure of H₂ in mmHg?
quiz.3.e: The total pressure in the container equals the outside pressure and is made up of the pressures of H₂ and water vapor. So the pressure of H₂ is 750 − 27 = 723 mmHg. Adding the water vapor pressure is a common mistake.
quiz.3.y.0: You subtract the water vapor pressure, you don't add it. The total pressure is the sum of the pressures of H₂ and water vapor.
quiz.3.y.1: 750 mmHg is the total pressure. It includes 27 mmHg of water vapor pressure, so the pressure of H₂ is less.
quiz.3.y.3: 27 mmHg is the partial pressure of the water vapor. The pressure of H₂ is the total minus this value.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Push the piston, heat the gas, add moles and discover the laws yourself.
A:adimlar.0.metin: With temperature and moles constant, push the piston to reduce the volume. The particles will hit the walls more often. Make the pressure 2 atm.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: When the volume was halved, the pressure doubled, and P·V always stayed 4. This is called Boyle's law, written P₁·V₁ = P₂·V₂.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Now the pressure is constant and the piston is free. The gas at 27 °C has a volume of 6 L. Heat the gas and make its volume 8 L. Also look at the temperature in kelvins.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: To raise the volume from 6 L to 8 L, that is by 4/3, the kelvin temperature must also go up by 4/3. It goes from 300 K to 400 K, or 127 °C. This is called Charles's law, written V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
A:adimlar.2.metin: This time the container is closed and its volume doesn't change. The gas inside is at 27 °C and 1 atm. We'll heat the container to 327 °C.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What happens to the pressure when the gas is heated to 327 °C?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The volume is constant, but the particles speed up and hit the walls more often and harder.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The kelvin temperature went from 300 K to 600 K, so it doubled. At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to kelvin temperature (P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). That's why you never throw a spray can into a fire.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Going from 27 to 327 looks like a 12-fold increase. But in gas calculations temperature is always in kelvins, and it goes from 300 K to 600 K.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The piston container holds 1 mol of gas at 27 °C, 24.6 L and 1 atm. Change the volume, temperature and moles, and the particles and pressure change instantly. Find three ways to double the pressure.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Make the pressure 2 atm without changing the temperature or the moles.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: You halved the volume (12.3 L) and the pressure doubled. P·V stayed constant, which is Boyle's law. The particles hit the walls more often.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Keep the volume at 24.6 L and heat the gas to 327 °C. What is the pressure now?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The temperature went from 300 K to 600 K. When the kelvin temperature doubled, the pressure doubled too, which is Gay-Lussac's law. The Celsius value went from 27 to 327, 12 times larger, but calculations use kelvins.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Find a third way to make the pressure 2 atm at 27 °C and 24.6 L.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: You made the moles 2. With twice as many particles in the same volume, there were twice as many hits on the walls. All three laws are contained in P·V = n·R·T.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Change the temperature and watch how the arrows and bars change.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: If the absolute temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K, what happens to the average kinetic energy?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature itself, not its square. Four times would need 1200 K.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature. When the temperature changes, it changes too.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature. Speed grows with √T, so at 600 K it is about 1.41 times larger.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Put cotton soaked in NH₃ at one end of a glass tube and cotton soaked in HCl at the other. Where the two gases meet, they form white NH₄Cl smoke.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Where does the white ring form?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: For the ring to form in the middle, the two gases would have to spread at the same rate. But their molar masses differ.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A light gas spreads faster, and r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁). NH₃ (17 g/mol) is about 1.47 times faster than HCl (36.5 g/mol) and covers 59% of the way. This is called Graham's law.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: That would mean HCl is faster. But HCl is heavier.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Each gas in a mixture exerts its own pressure. The container holds 2 mol of N₂ at a pressure of 1 atm. Add O₂ and make the O₂ pressure half of the total.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: 2 mol of O₂ also exerts 1 atm, and the total pressure becomes 1 + 1 = 2 atm. Partial pressure is proportional to mole fraction, so P(O₂) = X(O₂) · P(total) = ½ · 2 = 1 atm. This is called Dalton's law, written P(total) = P(A) + P(B).
A:kapanis.0: In gas calculations temperature is always in kelvins, found from T = t + 273.
A:kapanis.1: By Boyle's law, P·V is constant. By Charles's law V, and by Gay-Lussac's law P, is directly proportional to temperature. By Avogadro's law, V is proportional to moles.
A:kapanis.2: All these laws combine into P·V = n·R·T, with R = 0.082 L·atm/(mol·K).
A:kapanis.3: Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature. By Graham's law a light gas spreads faster, and the rate is inversely proportional to √M.
A:kapanis.4: By Dalton's law, the total pressure of a mixture is the sum of the partial pressures. Each gas's partial pressure is proportional to its mole fraction.
